title: Dual transmission hotspots: Behavioural interdependence amplifies disease risk from anthropogenic feeders in a communal roosting bird species
content:
Due to behavioral interdependence, wild turkeys aggregate at both anthropogenic feeders and linked roost sites. These congregations have the potential to create dual transmission hotspots, driving disease transmission during both daytime foraging and nighttime roosting


Abstract

Anthropogenic food sources (e.g. feeders) are known to facilitate wildlife disease transmission by aggregating animals during foraging. However, the full impact may be underestimated if behavioural interdependencies, which can increase risks beyond foraging, are not considered. Understanding how linked behaviours influence disease dynamics is essential to inform effective management. We investigated the role of foraging-roosting interdependence in shaping disease transmission risk using wild turkeys (Meleagris gallopavo), a communally roosting species, as a model system. We combined empirical GPS movement data (n = 21 females) with stochastic individual-based susceptible-infectious (SI) disease simulations to quantify contact patterns and transmission events relative to feeders. Turkey foraging at feeders was strongly linked to nighttime roost site selection; individuals visiting feeders were significantly more likely to roost near (<300 m), but not directly at, those feeders on the preceding and subsequent nights, leading to aggregations during both activities. This behavioural interdependence created distinct dual transmission hotspots: primary hotspots occurred directly at feeders during daytime foraging (>50% of simulated transmission), while significant secondary hotspots could occur at nearby roosting locations during the night (>10%–20% of simulated transmission) under scenarios with higher relative nighttime transmission probability, plausible for highly transmissible pathogens. Individual turkeys exhibiting stronger behavioural preferences for feeders consistently experienced higher simulated risks of both acquiring and transmitting infections across the various transmission probability scenarios. Practical implications. Behavioural interdependence can amplify wildlife disease risks associated with anthropogenic feeders by creating secondary transmission hotspots (e.g. at roost sites) distinct from the primary foraging locations, a mechanism relevant to many communally roosting species interacting with such resources. Consequently, evaluating and managing disease risks requires considering the landscape context of the entire feeder–roost complex and these linked behavioural effects, particularly for gregarious species utilizing supplemental food sources.
